questions.text: When you say you want more EMI-eligible purchases to convert, do you mean you want more transactions converted, or more value/amount converted into EMI — even if that means fewer but larger conversions?
questions.author: agent

contingency.ifA: Design targets volume: broad reach, easy low-friction conversions, message tuned to make converting feel simple regardless of ticket size.
contingency.ifB: Design targets value: prioritise larger eligible transactions and customers with bigger EMI-eligible balances, even if the total count of conversions is smaller.
contingency.ifUnknown: Default to counting conversions but flag that this favours small-ticket conversions, and ask again once the first run's data is in.

questions.text: Have you noticed any pattern in who already converts an eligible purchase to EMI on their own, or is that something you don't track?
questions.author: agent

contingency.ifA: Use the named pattern to decide who the campaign should focus on first.
contingency.ifB: Treat it as unknown and design the first run to also surface which segment converts, rather than assuming one.

questions.text: What do you believe is stopping the rest of the eligible purchases from being converted?
questions.author: agent

contingency.ifA: Build messaging and timing around the specific reason given (e.g. unaware of the option, cost concern, timing of the offer window).
contingency.ifB: If they say they don't know, widen the first run to test more than one plausible barrier rather than designing around a guess.

converters.shape: Transactions of ₹10,000 or more already convert to EMI on their own more often than smaller eligible transactions; the untapped volume sits in the sub-₹10,000 eligible purchases.

candidates.why: Manager has directly observed these convert to EMI on their own more often, per their own words.

barriers.statement: Customers don't realise a given purchase actually qualifies for EMI conversion, so they never act on it.
barriers.quote: i think they dont know if txn is eligibile for emi or not

strategy.summary: You want more eligible card purchases converted to EMI — counted as a number, not by rupee value. You've seen that ₹10,000+ eligible purchases already convert on their own more often; the untapped count sits in the smaller eligible purchases. Your read is that customers simply don't know a given purchase qualifies for EMI — that's an awareness gap, so the campaign's job is to say "this purchase can become EMI" clearly, repeatedly, and before the 7-day window closes. Every eligible purchase enters; the two amount bands get different pacing, not different access.
approach: Entry is every settled, customer-initiated, EMI-eligible transaction — this is the audience the manager asked for (everyone who still can convert), confirmed against the Transaction entity's own eligibility and status fields.
The ₹10,000 split comes directly from the manager's own observation, used only to pace messaging, not to exclude anyone.
The barrier (customers don't know a purchase qualifies) comes directly from the manager's belief, so the lever chosen is message content, not incentive or targeting.
Goal is the EMI Request reaching a Successful status — this is the only event in the platform that proves the behaviour actually happened, on a different entity than the entry trigger.

Since there's no campaign history, the day-0 message for the untapped (below ₹10,000) group is run as a genuine 50/50 wording test rather than a guess, because this is the only way to learn anything about what closes the awareness gap before scaling spend on it.

The 7-day campaign window and the use of SMS as a fallback/last-chance channel reflect the manager's stated window and the knowledge base's guidance on WhatsApp/SMS reach for Indian retail cardholders.
Transaction events and EMI status-change events are flagged by the platform itself as proposed, not confirmed live in production — carried as a limitation, not assumed working.
assumptions: A transaction counts as the moment of opportunity once it is SETTLED and marked EMI Eligible — EXPIRED/CANCELED transactions are excluded since the chance has already closed.
Initiated By is restricted to CUSTOMER_INITIATED so system-generated postings (fees, interest, reversals) never enter this journey.
The ₹10,000 boundary is read from the manager's own words, not a chosen threshold — transactions at or above ₹10,000 get the lighter path, below it get the fuller path.
No incentive (cashback, fee waiver) is assumed or offered in the copy — this is a pure awareness/clarity play per the stated barrier, not a pricing lever.
unknowns: Whether the Transaction and EMI_STATUS_CHANGED events are actually live and firing in production today — the platform marks both as proposed, not confirmed built.
Whether the wording test (functional vs benefit framing) actually produces a measurable difference in this population — this run is what tells us, not a prior belief.

Whether customers who don't convert even after all three touches are blocked by something other than awareness (e.g. not wanting the instalment structure) — this campaign cannot distinguish that from simple non-engagement.

architectures.name: Amount-paced awareness nudge with a wording experiment
architectures.audience: Every settled, customer-initiated, EMI-eligible transaction — paced differently by amount band.
architectures.timing: Below ₹10,000: day 0, day 2 (reactive to read status), day 5 last chance. ₹10,000+: day 0, day 4 reminder.
architectures.measurement: Conversion count by arm (functional vs benefit wording) and by amount band, read against this run's own baseline since none exists yet.
architectures.why: Puts the fuller sequence and the only wording test where the untapped count actually sits (below ₹10,000), while still messaging the self-converting ₹10,000+ group without over-spending effort there. Directly serves the manager's stated goal of maximising the count of conversions.
architectures.entry: Every settled, customer-initiated, EMI-eligible transaction — paced differently by amount band.
architectures.whyChosen: Puts the fuller sequence and the only wording test where the untapped count actually sits (below ₹10,000), while still messaging the self-converting ₹10,000+ group without over-spending effort there. Directly serves the manager's stated goal of maximising the count of conversions.

architectures.name: Uniform fixed-cadence reminder
architectures.audience: Every settled, customer-initiated, EMI-eligible transaction — one treatment for all.
architectures.timing: Fixed day 0 / day 3 / day 6 reminders for everyone, regardless of amount or engagement.
architectures.measurement: Only a single overall conversion count — no way to tell whether wording or pacing mattered.
architectures.why: Simpler to build, but ignores the one converter pattern the manager has actually seen, spends equal effort on a group that already converts well, and teaches nothing about which message works — a real cost on a first run meant to establish a baseline.
architectures.tradeOff: Lower build complexity, but no learning and likely fewer incremental conversions from the sub-₹10,000 group where the opportunity is concentrated.

rejected.why: Would spend equal messaging effort on the ₹10,000+ group that already converts on its own, and would not test any wording against another — a missed chance on a first run with zero prior data.

rejected.option: Excluding or down-weighting the ₹10,000+ group entirely
rejected.why: The manager's goal is counted conversions, not value — every eligible transaction, including large ones that haven't yet converted, still adds to that count, so they keep a path, just a lighter one.

rejected.option: Branching on merchant checkout type (online vs POS)
rejected.why: Manager confirmed this split doesn't need different treatment — closed per their own instruction to ignore it.

hypotheses: If customers are told plainly and promptly that a specific purchase qualifies for EMI, some who would otherwise never check will convert it — the barrier is awareness, not cost or trust.

A benefit-led framing (no-cost EMI, lighter on the wallet) may outperform a plain functional framing (you are eligible, convert here) for the sub-₹10,000 group, but this is untested and is exactly what the day-0 split is meant to find out.
measurement: Track conversion count (EMI Request reaching Successful) split by amount band and, within the below-₹10,000 band, by which day-0 wording arm the customer received.
Read the wording test as a simple comparison of conversion counts between the two day-0 arms — first time this bank will have this data, so treat it as the baseline, not a lift.
Watch how many conversions come from the day-2/day-5 reminders versus the day-0 message alone, to judge whether the reminders are earning their place or just adding cost without added conversions.
Without a held-out no-message control, this run can report what happened, not what the campaign caused — the builder's standard holdout is the only control in place here.

Since no campaign history exists, this run establishes the baseline conversion count rather than being judged against a prior number.

openItems.question: Are the Transaction event and the EMI status-change event actually live in production, or still in proposed/unbuilt state?
openItems.whyItMatters: Both the entry trigger and the goal for this entire campaign depend on these two events. If neither fires yet, nothing in this plan can run.
openItems.ifUnanswered: Flagging to the platform team before launch is assumed as a precondition; the plan is designed assuming they will be made live.

openItems.question: Is a 50/50 split acceptable for the day-0 wording test on the below-₹10,000 group?
openItems.whyItMatters: A different split would change how fast the test reaches a readable result, but not the design itself.
openItems.ifUnanswered: Default to 50/50, the platform's standard experiment split.

touches.path: Below ₹10,000 — functional framing (half of this group)
touches.purpose: First touch: tell the customer plainly that this purchase qualifies for EMI.
touches.ifStillUnconverted: If read but no action: gets a reinforcing WhatsApp reminder on day 2. If not read: gets the same fact resent on SMS on day 2.

touches.path: Below ₹10,000 — benefit framing (other half of this group)
touches.purpose: First touch testing a no-cost-EMI benefit framing against the functional one.
touches.ifStillUnconverted: If read but no action: gets a reinforcing WhatsApp reminder on day 2. If not read: gets the same fact resent on SMS on day 2.

touches.path: Below ₹10,000 — read but no action (either framing)
touches.purpose: Reinforce urgency now that we know the message was seen.
touches.ifStillUnconverted: Gets the final SMS last-chance message on day 5.

touches.path: Below ₹10,000 — did not read day-0 WhatsApp message
touches.purpose: Repeat the same eligibility fact on a different channel in case WhatsApp wasn't seen.
touches.ifStillUnconverted: Gets the final SMS last-chance message on day 5.

touches.purpose: Last chance before the 7-day window closes.
touches.ifStillUnconverted: No further message; campaign ends for them without conversion.

blueprint.description: Fires the moment a customer-initiated, settled transaction is flagged EMI-eligible. Splits by ticket size: below ₹10,000 gets a fuller reactive sequence with a wording test on the first message; ₹10,000 and above gets a lighter two-touch path since that group already converts more often on its own. Goal is the EMI request reaching Successful status, inside the 7-day request window.
